claims.text: MATERIAL NEW FINDING - THE REPORTS THE WAIVER ATTACHES TO HAVE LARGELY SUNSET. The Office of the Law Revision Counsel carries a statutory note under 10 U.S.C. 119 headed 'Termination of Reporting Requirements' which reads verbatim: 'For termination, effective Dec. 31, 2021, of provisions in subsecs. (a) and (b) of this section requiring submittal of annual report to Congress, see section 1061 of Pub. L. 114-328, set out as a note under section 111 of this title.' The annual special access program report under 119(a) and the new-program notice and justification report under 119(b) therefore terminated as statutory requirements on 31 December 2021. After that date the only report to which the 119(e)(1) waiver can attach is the 119(c) report on a planned classification change or public declassification announcement. This reshapes the board's question: for activity after 31 December 2021 there may be no 119(a) or 119(b) report in existence to waive information out of, which would make the absence of any 119(e)(2) delivery unsurprising rather than suspicious for that window - while for the period 1988 through 2021 the reports were mandatory and the waiver machinery was live.

This is the legal definition of a 'waived' SAP.

claims.nodeLabel: 10 U.S.C. 119 - Special Access Programs: Congressional Oversight
claims.text: Because every duty in section 119 is imposed on 'the Secretary of Defense', a program deliberately concealed from the Secretary of Defense generates no identifiable statutory violation by any named official. Reasoning: the statute has one obligor and no strict-liability provision reaching subordinate program managers or contractors.

claims.nodeLabel: 10 U.S.C. 119 - Special Access Programs: Congressional Oversight

Reasoning: (e) waives only (a),(b),(c); the sunset note names only (a) and (b). Whether DoD continued the report voluntarily is not established by any record located here.

claims.text: The waiver authority is vested in the Secretary of Defense personally and is conditioned only on the Secretary's own determination of adverse national security effect; the statute prescribes no finding of fact, no time limit, no periodic re-justification, and no congressional ability to disapprove.

claims.nodeLabel: 10 U.S.C. 119(e) - Waiver of SAP Reporting (the 'waived SAP' authority)

claims.nodeLabel: 10 U.S.C. 119(e) - Waiver of SAP Reporting (the 'waived SAP' authority)
claims.text: Because (e)(1) reaches only 'any requirement ... that certain information be included in a report,' a plain reading is that the Secretary may strip content out of the reports but may not skip the (f) 30-day pre-initiation notification of the program's existence. A program whose existence was never notified to the defense committees at all would therefore not be a lawfully 'waived' SAP under section 119 but an unreported one. Reasoning stated from the text of (e)(1) and (f).

claims.nodeLabel: 10 U.S.C. 119(e) - Waiver of SAP Reporting (the 'waived SAP' authority)
claims.text: Read literally, 119(g) names six bodies - Senate Armed Services, Senate Appropriations, the Defense Subcommittee of Senate Appropriations, and the three House counterparts - so 'the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' is up to twelve members, not eight. The conventional 'Gang of Eight' framing for defense waived programs counts only the four parent committees. Reasoning: statutory text versus practice convention.

claims.nodeLabel: 50 U.S.C. 2426 - Congressional Oversight of DOE/NNSA Special Access Programs
claims.text: The NNSA Administrator can lawfully initiate a special access program with no advance notice to any congressional committee, because the waiver in 2426(e)(1) expressly reaches the report-and-wait requirement of 2426(f); the Secretary of Defense cannot, because 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(1) reaches only subsections (a), (b) and (c). Reasoning: direct textual comparison of the two waiver provisions.

claims.nodeLabel: 50 U.S.C. 3093 - Presidential Approval and Reporting of Covert Actions
claims.text: An activity characterised as covert action is reportable to no defense committee at all, and under 3093(c)(3) need not be reported to anyone in advance - making it the only regime weaker on prior notice than a waived DoD special access program. Reasoning: 3093 runs solely to the intelligence committees or the Gang of Eight, and (c)(3) removes even that.

claims.sourceText: 32 CFR 117.3(b) read against 10 U.S.C. 119 and 50 U.S.C. 3348(g)(3)

Reasoning: all four reporting statutes are triggered by the term 'special access program', which ACCM expressly is not.

Reasoning: each element is individually lawful and the composition has never been tested against a UAP-specific demand.

claims.text: Because the annual SAP report to Congress uses only unclassified nicknames, a member reading the list sees a word, not a mission. Reasoning: DoDI 5205.11 para 5.d expressly directs nickname use in the annual report and leaves the codeword optional and classified.

claims.locator: e), EO 13526 sec. 4.3(b)(3) and 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3) together
claims.nodeLabel: Executive Order 13526 - Classified National Security Information
claims.sourceText: Reading of 10 U.S.C. 119(e), EO 13526 sec. 4.3(b)(3) and 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3) together; all three texts read from primary sources on 22 August 2026
claims.text: Three separate instruments each narrow oversight of the same object, and none of them depends on the others. 10 U.S.C. 119(e) reduces the congressional readership of a waived SAP to twelve members. EO 13526 sec. 4.3(b)(3) can reduce ISOO's access to one person. 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3) relieves the Director, DCSA of NISP industrial-security oversight entirely on a carve-out. Congressional, executive and industrial-security oversight are narrowed by three different authorities, so closing any one of them would leave the other two intact.

claims.nodeLabel: FY2024 Intelligence Authorization Act sec. 7343 - Funding Limitations Relating to UAP
claims.sourceText: Public Law 118-31 secs. 1687 and 7343, read against 10 U.S.C. 119(e)
claims.text: Sections 1687 and 7343 together create a subject-matter exception that overrides the ordinary compartment logic: for UAP specifically, disclosure to a named list of committees and leaders is a condition of spending, regardless of whether the program is acknowledged, unacknowledged or waived. Reasoning: neither section contains a saving clause for programs whose reporting has been waived under 10 U.S.C. 119(e).

claims.nodeLabel: Howard P. "Buck" McKeon
claims.text: The chairman and ranking minority member of the House Armed Services Committee are among the twelve offices entitled under 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) to receive information withheld from a section 119 report and the Secretary of Defense's justification for the waiver.

claims.nodeLabel: Intelligence Community special access program control office enterprise
claims.sourceText: Inference from the scope of 10 U.S.C. 119 read against AARO's three-enterprise description
claims.text: A program carried in the IC control-office enterprise would not appear in the 10 U.S.C. 119 report to the defense committees, which means a member relying on the DoD SAP list cannot rule out its existence. claims.text: WHAT SHOULD EXIST IF THE WAIVER WERE BEING USED, AND WHY NONE OF IT IS PUBLIC. Four artefacts are implied by the statute and the DoD instruction: (i) the underlying 119(a), (b) or (c) report itself, which is classified and, for (a) and (b), no longer statutorily required after 31 December 2021; (ii) the Secretary's case-by-case determination that inclusion would adversely affect national security, which 119(e)(1) requires to be made but does not require to be recorded in any publicly indexed form; (iii) the withheld information plus a written justification delivered jointly to twelve named members, which by the Moynihan Commission's account has historically been delivered orally; and (iv) the SAPOC annual review record of whether each waived program should retain that status, which is internal to the Department. The absence of a public instance is therefore fully explained by the design of the mechanism and is NOT evidence of concealment beyond what the statute itself authorises.
